title: Hearth. Design a home with your agent.
pitch: A 3D interior-design studio humans and AI agents share. 40 WebMCP tools let your agent read rooms, place and resize furniture, import floor plans, shop a real Shopify catalog, and prep checkout.
about_excerpt: A 3D interior-design studio humans and AI agents share. 40 WebMCP tools let your agent read rooms, place and resize furniture, import floor plans, shop a real Shopify catalog, and prep checkout. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GIF Agent placing furniture, arranging, comparing layouts Living room at golden hour with catalog, inspector and activity log The Tools panel listing the WebMCP tools and schemas A home built from an uploaded floor plan, furnished The import sheet reading a floor-plan image Resized sofa and size-matched catalog results The import sheet reading a floor-plan image Resized sofa and size-matched catalog results Ghost preview of a Shopify product plus the cart Door-swing and clearance conflict diagrams with a fix Accessibility mode with turning circles and paths Exported design board Whole-home framing The seven floor-plan templates plus "Import your own plan" Orbit camera view Inspiration I was thinking of buying a home, and one question that kept coming was how will I furnish it. The hard question was not the price. It was: will the furniture fit, and will the door still open? Where should I place the furniture, will it look good as per my home layout, and what will be the total cost I might need. An AI agent should be able to help with this, but it can't. A chat model can't see the room. A screen-scraping agent can guess at pixels, but it can't measure a wall, and it certainly can't be trusted to drag a sofa. Room planners exist (IKEA Kreativ, Planner 5D); none of them let an agent in. Browser agents exist; none of them can measure a wall. When I read the WebMCP proposal the idea clicked: instead of making the agent reverse-engineer my page, I could hand it the same verbs I use. Interior design felt like the perfect test. It's spatial, iterative, visual, and it ends with a real purchase. So I built Hearth: a 3D home studio where a person and an agent work on the same rooms, and the agent gets forty real tools instead of a screenshot. What it does Hearth is a shared interior-design studio. You get a dollhouse-style 3D home you can drag furniture around in, with magnetic snapping and live dimension lines. Your agent gets the same home through tools registered on the page with document.modelContext.registerTool . It reads the space as data: rooms, walls and their free spans, door swings, every item in centimetres, and a conflict report (clearances, traffic paths, blocked doors) with a one-line fix for each. It designs with semantic anchors, so "put the sofa against the north wall facing the window" becomes move_furniture {anchor:{wall:"north", facing:"window:…"}} and no coordinates cross the conversation. It can arrange a room for a purpose, change the time of day, and turn on accessibility mode (90 cm paths, 150 cm turning circles) and then fix what that flags. It can also build the home. Pick one of seven floor plans, or drop a photo of your own and call import_floor_plan : a vision model reads room names, printed dimensions, doors and windows, and Hearth's layout engine turns that into a to-scale scene with shared walls snapped, doors paired across them, and starter furniture that arrives conflict-free. Every placed item has an exact size, resize_furniture changes it, and search_catalog ranks real Shopify products by closeness to that size and says whether each match is exact, close or off, with the centimetre delta. The shop is a live Shopify store with 71 products. The agent can filter by what fits a wall, ghost-preview a product in the room in a colourway, add it to the cart and hand you the checkout link. The purchase click stays yours, which is the only version of agent shopping I would actually use. A typical session: drop a photo of the flat and get a furnished home to scale; ask for a sofa that fits the north wall under $800 and watch it ghost into the room; confirm it, add it to the cart, take the checkout link. Nothing in that chain needs a coordinate or a product id from me. Everything is visible and reversible. Save layouts and compare two with a slider, undo anything, clear the home and restore it, export a design board. When the agent acts, an orb flies to the spot, a receipt lands in the activity log with the exact tool input and result, and an Undo chip appears. Destructive tools open a confirmation dialog in the page, and if I decline, the agent gets {error:"cancelled", detail:"The human declined…"} back, so it knows why, not just that it failed. How I built it I wrote the contracts before the code. TOOLS.md specifies every tool's name, description, parameters, result shape, group and gate; SCENE_SCHEMA.md pins the scene graph, units and coordinate frame. Everything else was judged against those two files. The stack is Next.js 16 and React 19 with React-Three-Fiber for the scene. A zustand store tags every mutation human or agent , and a pure TypeScript geometry engine (walls, clearances, traffic paths, floor-plan layout) has no React or three.js in it and is covered by a few hundred unit tests. The shop is the Shopify Storefront API; the floor-plan reader and the fallback assistant use the OpenAI Responses API through server-only route handlers. It runs in ChatGPT desktop's built-in browser, in Chrome with WebMCP enabled (the production origin ships an origin-trial token), and where a browser has no WebMCP yet, an in-page assistant drives the same tools through Chrome's polyfill. The WebMCP layer is one registry, src/tools/registry.ts . The surface I use: registerTool with an AbortSignal per group, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, the toolchange event and getTools() mirrored into a Tools panel so a judge can inspect the surface without an agent, executeTool through the polyfill for the fallback assistant, and Chrome's published budgets as CI assertions. Each tool is defined once with a zod schema and converted to JSON Schema. The registry asserts the budgets at definition time (names ≤ 30 chars, descriptions ≤ 500, parameter descriptions ≤ 150) and the test suite asserts every result stays under 1,500 characters across three scene fixtures. 29 tools register synchronously on load so DevTools and Lighthouse see them cold. 11 more live in four state-gated groups (build, preview, variants, checkout), each behind its own AbortController . When the scene changes the registry diffs the desired groups and registers or aborts, and any tool whose result changes the gate set ( set_mode , but also update_cart opening checkout or preview_in_room opening preview) waits for the registry to settle and returns tools_ready . Results are plain JSON envelopes. Success carries the room, the conflicts and a hint. Failure carries an error code, a detail and a suggestion; a blocked placement adds the free wall spans, an unknown id adds the three closest candidates, so the model can self-correct instead of retrying blindly. Every room , item or product parameter accepts an id or a name, item accepts selected , and room_id -style keys are
video_transcript_excerpt: This is Heart. It's a home interior design studio where you and your agent can collaborate to design your house. You can select from the different layouts that they are present, or you can even upload an image of your floor plan and design it. You can view your home from different angles or a different view, or focus on a particular room, and then design it as you want. But, the interesting part is not what you can do. It's that your agent can do all the same things that you can using the Web MCP tools that Heart registers on this page. I have opened Heart in the Codex desktop application. I'm going to give it a simple task of adding one more chair in the living room, which faces opposite the first chair. Let's see how it does. So, the agent first used different tools to first inspect the room, and then it added the chair using the tools. Now, let's give this agent a more difficult task. I have this image of a floor plan with me. I'm going to copy it and paste it into the chat, and I'm going to tell the agent to create a unfurnished home, which is as per this plan, and let's see what happens. So, the agent was able to create the house from the floor map using the Web MCP tools. Now, let's ask it to design this house and put in some sofa and bedrooms with some constraints like I want a sofa under $700 and two beds under $700 each. Now, the agent is aware of the dimensions of the house, and even the furniture is not uh just a toy furniture. It's coming from a real Shopify store that I created for this application. And then the agent will be able to put those things those furniture here and it will also be able to add it to the cart. Let's see how it goes. So as you can see the agent was able to put the furniture in the house. Here is the complete list of furniture that is available and the agent was able to pick the one as per my constraints. Now I can drag this furniture around. I can select a particular room and I can design it or I can ask my AI agent to design this room. Also I had asked the agent to put the furniture into the cart and here the furniture is present in the cart. I hope you like this demo and I hope you get some time to play with heart and design your home. Thank you.

live_observation.first_impression: A 3D Hearth Studio room editor opens on a Living Room with Design mode, lighting/view controls, a large catalog, inspector, activity, cart, and agent-oriented quick actions.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked Start designing on the welcome card.
live_observation.after_state: The welcome card disappeared and the full room-design workspace remained available, including catalog items, room controls, activity, and cart panels.
live_observation.notes: The catalog and room editor were immediately visible; the agent tools control reported unavailable in this context.
